paras: The police clubbing of a 15th Infantry soldier at a Lenox Avenue tailor shop took place in Harlem, New York City, on or about June 20, 1919, when Officer Collins of the 38th precinct beat a soldier over the head and arrested him for assault. A crowd of about 1,000 gathered in protest, and the Chicago Defender reported the episode on its front page under a headline saying citizens had been aroused by the policeman's conduct.

The man, whose name is printed in the badly garbled text as both 'Arthrochleon' and 'George', was described as a former member of the 369th Infantry, now of the 15th Infantry; the Defender did not state his race.

According to the police, he entered the tailor shop of Samuel Schleifer at 615 Lenox Avenue to try on a custom-made coat, and a dispute over money followed among him, the tailor and the policeman. The police said he drew a knife, which he denied, and Officer Collins charged that he punched him in the nose three times. While the officer was beating him over the head, about 1,000 people gathered and protested; he was taken to Harlem hospital and treated for a scalp wound.

He was then arrested and charged with what the OCR renders as 'follicious' [felonious] assault. Soldiers of the 15th and residents collected witnesses' names, and angry crowds denounced the attack until late Friday while police guarded the shop. Some hours after the guard was withdrawn, the man's sympathizers wrecked the tailor shop.
No report of the outcome of the assault charge or of any action against Officer Collins was found in the coverage.

The only known account is a New York dispatch dated June 20 that the Chicago Defender ran on page one of its June 21 issue under the headline 'Citizens, Aroused by Conduct of Bluecoat, to Take Action.' The Defender said the soldier was 'clubbed unmercifully' and called the beating a 'dismal act', yet it also set out the police version, including the officer's charge that he had been punched.

reader.title: Police clubbing of a 15th Infantry soldier at a Lenox Avenue tailor shop
bases: A single patrolman, Officer Collins of the 38th precinct, beat a man over the head with his club during a dispute in a tailor shop and then arrested him (A1).
Only one Chicago Defender dispatch (A1) reports the clubbing; no other Black-press account was found.

accounts.label: Police version
accounts.gist: A dispute over money and a custom-made coat led the man to draw a knife and punch Officer Collins in the nose three times.

accounts.label: Victim and neighborhood witnesses
accounts.gist: The man denied drawing a knife; soldiers and residents said he was 'clubbed unmercifully' and collected names of witnesses.

framing.detail: The Chicago Defender ran the dispatch on page one under 'Citizens, Aroused by Conduct of Bluecoat, to Take Action', calling the beating 'unmerciful' and a 'dismal act', while still giving the police account.

conflicts.note: Both names appear in the same garbled article for what reads as one man; the true name cannot be recovered from the OCR.

versions.value: Police: he drew a knife and punched the officer three times

conflicts.note: Only the police account of the punches is given; the knife claim is denied by the victim.

info: On or about Friday, June 20, 1919 (dispatch dated New York, June 20; crowd remained 'until a late hour Friday')
Tailor shop of Samuel Schleifer, 615 Lenox Avenue, near 141st Street, Harlem, New York City
One man, a former member of the 369th Infantry now of the 15th Infantry, named in the garbled text as 'Arthrochleon' and then as 'George'; the two names appear to refer to the same man
Police said he drew a knife (which he denied) and punched the officer in the nose three times; he was charged with 'follicious' [felonious] assault

sources.note: Only report: New York dispatch of June 20; soldier clubbed by Officer Collins after a dispute in a Lenox Avenue tailor shop; crowd of about 1,000; shop later wrecked. OCR heavily garbled.
